new_statements.quote: there exists clear evidence of a system of pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence. [...] Smith River has pitch with these sharply limited distributions: a) All monosyllabic utterances, such as duu no and su? good, have high pitch. b) Every utterance has at least one high pitch. c) There are no polysyllabic utterances containing all high or all low pitches. d) Within a word, as tentatively identified, the maximum number of high pitches is two. [...] In summary, the Smith River suprasegmental system shows similarities to what has been called a pitch-accent system, in contrast with a pitch system like that of Navaho
new_statements.citation: Bright, Jane O. 1964. The Phonology of Smith River Athapaskan (Tolowa). International Journal of American Linguistics 30(2):101-107.
new_statements.locator: p. 104, section 3 (suprasegmentals); identity remark p. 101, section 0
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK (confirmed): Re-opened (p.104 block, file lines ~260-303; two-column interleave) and cross-checked against a fresh extracted text of and the slice3 copy. All three quoted stretches are present word for word at sec. 3, p.104: 'there exists clear evidence of a system of pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence'; 'Unlike the Apachean and Northern Athapaskan languages, Smith River has pitch with these sharply limited distributions: a) All monosyllabic utterances, such as duu no and su? good, have high pitch. b) Every utterance has at least one high pitch. c) There are no polysyllabic utterances containing all high or all low pitches. d) Within a word, as tentati…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tolowa(-Chetco) has a pitch-accent system: prominence is realised as high pitch, every word/utterance carries at least one high-pitched syllable and a word carries at most two, but the source gives no rule locating the accented syllable by position, weight or morphology; accent position must be learned per word (contrasting pairs such as baasag 'bread' vs baaseh 'seagulls' are listed). Later work (Tuttle 1990 apud Doty & Guion 2007) reanalyses the same prominence as stress accent, again without a published placement rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Bright allows up to two high pitches within a word (constraint d) but does not rank them; Doty & Guion 2007 transcribe one 4-syllable word with primary on the penult and a secondary on the initial. No rule stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; Bright notes words are only 'tentatively identified'. Jacobs & Seaburg 1976 note that stress marks in the 1935 Chetco field transcription are unreliable (slash ambiguous between length and stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Bright's constraints a-c are phrased over utterances, d over the word; her contrasting pairs are citation forms. The description is of the Smith River (Tolowa, California) dialect; Chetco (Oregon) is named on p.101 as an almost mutually intelligible northern dialect and is not separately described. Community orthography (Bommelyn et al. 1972/1983, covering 'Smith River, Chetco, Tututni') marks the stressed syllable word by word with a diacritic, consistent with non-predictable placement.
new_statements.identity_note: chet1237 is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code: Glottolog states Chetco and Tolowa 'are indistinguishable as languages' (citing Bommelyn 1997) and redirects to Tolowa-Chetco [tol] = tolo1259, which is ALREADY a catalog unit ( row tolo1259, coded from Bright 1964:104). The only first-hand prosodic statement is Bright 1964, which describes the Smith River (Tolowa proper, California) dialect and itself says Smith River is 'almost mutually intelligible with the more northern Athapaskan dialects spoken along the Winchuck and Chetco rivers' (p.101) -- i.e. it does not describe the Chetco dialect directly. For the Chetco dialect proper (Billy Metcalf, Siletz 1935), the only linguistic publications (Jacobs 1968; Jacobs & Seaburg 1976/1977) are texts whose introduction notes that stress was marked in the field transcription but gives no rule. Bommelyn et al.'s community textbook titles the language 'The Tolowa (Smith River, Chetco, Tututni) Language'. Adding chet1237 as its own catalog entry would double-count tolo1259 (retired codes confer no identity).

sources.locator: p. 104, section 3 (suprasegmentals); identity remark p. 101, section 0
sources.note: p.104 sec.3: 'pitch accent or tone, with at least two degrees of prominence'; high pitch limited by constraints a-d (monosyllables high; every utterance >=1 high; no all-high/all-low polysyllables; max two highs per word); summarised as 'a pitch-accent system, in contrast with a pitch system like that of Navaho'. No statement of where the accent falls; p.101 places Chetco-river speech as a near-identical northern dialect.

sources.note: ch.1 fn.2: 'Quasi-tonal phenomena are found in the Oregon languages. Bright (1964) described a pitch accent system for Tolowa'; ch.4 sec.3.2 'Chetco' treats only segmental diagnostics (nasalization, coda tɬ, dž) vs Tututni; nothing on Chetco stress.

sources.citation: Doty, Christopher S. & Susan G. Guion. 2007. Tolowa Peak Pitch Alignment. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 33:106-117. doi:10.3765/bls.v33i1.3521.
sources.note: pp.106-107: 'Tolowa was first described as having pitch accent, which was realized as high pitch on various syllables (Bright 1964). Subsequent work... seemed to indicate that Tolowa was perhaps better thought of as having stress accent... (Tuttle 1990)'; 'unstressed syllables... do not carry pitch accent'; 'both stress and pitch accent may be relevant'. Instrumental; no placement rule; stressed syllables in their token table are word-initial in most disyllables, final in some.

sources.note: fn.6 (p.332): glottal insertion results from 'an interaction between the system of pitch-accent and lengthening' -- presupposes a pitch-accent system; nothing on placement; no mention of Chetco.

sources.citation: Jacobs, Elizabeth D. & William R. Seaburg. [1976]. A Chetco Athabaskan Text and Translation. 17-pp. typescript (pp. 247-263 of a conference preprint volume); published as IJAL 43(4):269-273 (1977), doi:10.1086/465498.
sources.note: Sec.3 (p.248): in Jacobs' 1935 handwritten transcription 'it was sometimes difficult to determine... whether a particular slash indicated vowel length, stress, or the dot on an i'; 'irregularities... especially those of vowel length and stress, have been preserved as originally transcribed.' Stress marks exist in the Chetco text; no placement rule or analysis.

sources.citation: Bommelyn, Loren, et al. 1972 [ERIC record date; internal edition dated November 1983]. The Tolowa Language ('The Tolowa (Smith River, Chetco, Tututni) Language'). Arcata, CA: Center for Community Development, Humboldt State University. ERIC ED287617, 339 pp.
sources.note: Pronunciation key (PDF p.18, 'Key to Indian-Unifon punctuation and pronunciation'): 'A diagonal mark over a syllable shows that that syllable is stressed when the word is spoken.' Stress is marked word by word in the Unifon spelling (e.g. XUS WE-YO', NI-POS); no rule of placement given.
